source.author: stat
source.text: Continuo discors vario sententia motu scinditur: his Thebas tumidumque ambire Creonta, his placet Actaeae si quid clementia gentis adnuat; extremum curarum ac turpe reverti, hic non femineae subitum virtutis amorem colligit Argia, sexuque immane relicto tractat opus: placet egregii spes dura pericli! comminus infandi leges accedere regni, quo Rhodopes non ulla nurus nec alumna nivosi Phasidis innuptis vallata cohortibus iret.
source.text_original: Continuo discors vario sententia motu / scinditur: his Thebas tumidumque ambire Creonta, / his placet Actaeae si quid clementia gentis / adnuat; extremum curarum ac turpe reverti, / hic non femineae subitum virtutis amorem / colligit Argia, sexuque immane relicto / tractat opus: placet — egregii spes dura pericli! — / comminus infandi leges accedere regni, / quo Rhodopes non ulla nurus nec alumna nivosi / Phasidis innuptis vallata cohortibus iret.
source.text_english: At once the divided debate is split by shifting opinion: to some it seems right to surround Thebes and proud Creon, to others to see whether the mercy of the Actaean people will grant something; the end of their anxieties and shameful to return—here Argia gathers together no sudden love of womanly courage, and, leaving her sex behind in monstrous fashion, takes up the task. The harsh hope of outstanding danger pleases them: to go face to face toward the laws of that dreadful kingdom, where no daughter of Rhodope nor foster-child of snowy Phasis, surrounded by unmarried troops, would go.

reuse.author: val
reuse.text: Prima deum magnis canimus freta pervia natis fatidicamque ratem, Scythici quae Phasidis oras ausa sequi mediosque inter iuga concita cursus rumpere flammifero tandem consedit Olympo.
reuse.text_original: Prima deum magnis canimus freta pervia natis / fatidicamque ratem, Scythici quae Phasidis oras / ausa sequi mediosque inter iuga concita cursus / rumpere flammifero tandem consedit Olympo.
reuse.text_english: First we sing of the sea passages made traversable by the great sons of the gods, and of the prophetic ship, which, daring to follow the Scythian shores of Phasis and, driven on, to break through its course amid the middle mountain ridges, at last settled on fiery Olympus.
